title: Sanatana asks: who am I?
hookLine: a minister walks out of jail to ask one question, and two Hindu schools answer it two ways
carry: the self: krishna's ray, or brahman itself
tomorrow: why would a king pick up a broom?

lines: OUT OF JAIL, ACROSS THE FORESTS.
cards: Personality quizzes promise an answer in a few clicks. Sanatana wants a real one. He's Rupa's brother, a minister to the ruler of Bengal, and he's been locked up for trying to leave his post.
He pays off the jailer, crosses the forests on foot to Kashi, and falls at Chaitanya's feet. His question isn't about prison or politics. People call me learned, he says, and I believed them.

teach.h: A SERVANT, LIKE A RAY OF THE SUN.
teach.b: Chaitanya's answer, in paraphrase: by nature, the living being is an eternal servant of Krishna; a part of his power, one with him and also other than him, the way a ray belongs to the sun, or a spark to a fire.
Hear that view at its strongest. A ray really is sunlight; it's no stranger to the sun. But it isn't the sun.
That leaves room for a relationship, and a relationship leaves room for love. If there were no difference at all, who would be loving whom? In this book, bhakti isn't only something a person does.
Now the other answer, also from inside Hinduism, held by Advaita Vedanta, the school that follows Shankara. Its strongest case: an Upanishad says, that thou art.

teach.h: A RAY AND ITS SUN, OR THE SEA ITSELF?
teach.b: The self, at bottom, isn't a part of Brahman but Brahman itself; feeling like a small, separate someone is the confusion to be cleared. Hear the comfort in that. Nothing essential is ever far away.
It was never other. Devotion has a place in this view too, as something that clears the mind. Both schools read the same Upanishads, and both take Sanatana's question seriously.
One answers with a relationship: a ray and its sun. The other answers with an identity: a wave that turns out to be the sea. Hindu teachers still argue it, warmly.

how: Gaudiya Vaishnavas teach the self as Krishna's servant, one with and different from him; Advaita Vedantins teach that the self is Brahman. Both schools study the Upanishads and the Vedanta sutras.

o: a secret code for getting out of jail
a belief that the self is a passing illusion
devotion as what a person is, made for love

games.q: one question, two answers — tap the pairs.
p: a minister who asked: who am I?
a servant, like a ray of the sun
an Upanishad line both schools read

s: Hindus all believe the self is simply God
Advaita says the self is Brahman; Chaitanya's tradition says a servant, one with and other than Krishna, like a ray.
Sanatana was a minister who got out of prison to ask his question
he paid the jailer and crossed the forests to Kashi.
in Chaitanya's answer, the ray and the sun are exactly the same
a ray is sunlight, but it isn't the sun: one with, and other than.

games.q: you lean toward Chaitanya's answer. a friend asks you to give Advaita's best case, fairly. which do you say?
o: nothing essential is ever far away: the self was never other than Brahman.
it lets people skip practice and devotion altogether.
it's the newer view, so it must be the more developed one.
games.why: Advaita's strongest case is closeness: the separate self is the confusion, and Brahman was never far. devotion still has a place in it.

practice: Close your eyes if that's comfortable, and let Sanatana's question ride gently on the breath: who am I? Don't hurry an answer. Let the question rest the way sunlight rests on a floor, warm and unhurried, for the whole sit.

wordCard.voice: Bhakti, in Chaitanya's answer: not only what a person does, but what a person is, a ray made for shining.

orig.note: Sanskrit tat tvam asi, that thou art, from the Chandogya Upanishad; Advaita reads it as identity, other schools read it otherwise.

carryVoice: Your line: the self, Krishna's ray or Brahman itself. Two Hindu answers to Sanatana's question. Two days of the book to go.

sources.ref: Chaitanya Charitamrita, Madhya-lila 20 (Sanatana imprisoned, pays the jailer, crosses the forest, meets Chaitanya in Kashi; his questions: who am I, people call me learned; the answer: the living being is by nature Krishna's eternal servant, his marginal power, one and different, like the sun's ray or a fire's sparks)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7 (tat tvam asi, that thou art), as read in Advaita Vedanta
